topics.name: Tectonic Plates
topics.description: Earth's outer layer is divided into plates that move and interact at their boundaries.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Relate earthquakes near plate boundaries to movement and the release of stress.
evidence: Relates some earthquakes and mountain building to movement at plate boundaries.
misconceptions: Continents and the ocean floor never move.
topics.question: Why are many earthquakes found near tectonic plate boundaries?
topics.answer: Plates move and interact there, releasing energy when rocks slip.
topics.explanation: Plate movement can build stress in rocks; sudden movement can produce earthquakes.
hints: Think about where plates meet.
What can happen when movement suddenly releases stored stress?
topics.activity: Slide two pieces of paper past each other to model a plate boundary; label the model's limitations.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Chromosomes, Genes & DNA
topics.description: Genes are sections of DNA carried on chromosomes and contribute to inherited characteristics.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Locate genes as sections of DNA on chromosomes.
evidence: Connects genes, DNA and chromosomes in an explanation of inheritance.
misconceptions: Genes and chromosomes are unrelated structures.
topics.question: Where are genes found in a cell?
topics.answer: Genes are sections of DNA on chromosomes.
topics.explanation: Chromosomes package DNA; genes are particular stretches of that DNA.
hints: Start with the material DNA.
What structures carry the DNA?
topics.activity: Draw a cell nucleus, a chromosome and an enlarged short section labelled as a gene.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: The Nervous System
topics.description: The nervous system detects information and sends signals that help coordinate responses.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Describe how receptors and nerve signals help coordinate a response to heat.
evidence: Identifies a receptor, a signal pathway and a response in a simple example.
misconceptions: A muscle detects every stimulus and decides on its own how the body responds.
topics.question: What helps a person quickly move a hand away from an unexpectedly hot surface?
topics.answer: Receptors detect the heat and the nervous system signals muscles to move the hand.
topics.explanation: Sensory information and nerve signals coordinate a response; the muscles then contract.
hints: Which body system carries signals?
What acts after the signal reaches a muscle?
topics.activity: Draw a simple labelled pathway from a skin receptor to the nervous system and a hand muscle.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Body temperature regulation
topics.description: The body responds to temperature changes in ways that help keep internal conditions within a suitable range.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain how evaporation of sweat helps cool the body.
evidence: Names a response that helps the body lose heat.
misconceptions: Sweating raises body temperature by adding water to skin.
topics.question: How can sweating help the body cool down?
topics.answer: Evaporation of sweat from the skin transfers energy away from the body.
topics.explanation: Evaporation requires energy, which is taken from the skin and helps cool it.
hints: Think about what happens as sweat dries.
Evaporation takes energy from the skin.
topics.activity: Draw a flow diagram linking a hot body, sweating, evaporation and cooling.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: How Breathing Works
topics.description: Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs as the chest changes shape.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Biological Science > Year 2 knowledge
objectives: Identify air entering the lungs during breathing in.
evidence: Describes air entering the lungs as the chest expands.
misconceptions: People breathe food into their lungs to get energy.
topics.question: What enters the lungs when you breathe in?
topics.answer: Air enters the lungs through the nose or mouth.
topics.explanation: Breathing brings air into the body; food enters through the digestive system.
hints: Think about what moves through your nose and mouth when you breathe.
It is a gas mixture around you.
topics.activity: Place a hand on your chest and quietly notice how it moves during normal breathing.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Herbivores, Carnivores & Omnivores
topics.description: Animals obtain nutrition in different ways; herbivores eat plants or algae, carnivores eat animals and omnivores eat both.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Biological Science > Year 3 knowledge
objectives: Classify an animal as an omnivore from its diet.
evidence: Classifies a described animal diet using the foods eaten.
misconceptions: All animals eat the same kind of food.
topics.question: An animal eats both plants and other animals. What is its diet called?
topics.answer: It is an omnivore.
topics.explanation: Omnivores eat both plant and animal foods, unlike animals that eat only plants or only animals.
hints: Look at both kinds of food.
Which group eats both?
topics.activity: Sort animal picture cards by the foods described in a reliable reference.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Food, water and growth
topics.description: People need water and a range of nutrients from varied foods to grow, move and repair their bodies.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Biological Science > Year 3 knowledge
objectives: Explain why people need water and nutrients from a variety of foods.
evidence: Identifies variety and water as parts of meeting nutritional needs.
misconceptions: One food provides everything everyone needs to stay healthy.
topics.question: Why do people need a variety of foods and water?
topics.answer: Different foods provide different nutrients, and the body also needs water.
topics.explanation: Nutrients support processes such as growth and repair; no single example food should be treated as a complete diet.
hints: Do all foods provide the same nutrients?
Different foods contribute different things.
topics.activity: Create a pretend meal using varied food pictures and add a glass of water.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Arteries and veins
topics.description: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood back towards it.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish veins from arteries by the direction of blood flow relative to the heart.
evidence: Uses direction relative to the heart to distinguish an artery from a vein.
misconceptions: All arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and all veins carry oxygen-poor blood.
topics.question: Which blood vessels carry blood back towards the heart?
topics.answer: Veins.
topics.explanation: The distinction is based on the direction of blood flow relative to the heart, not simply its oxygen level.
hints: Focus on the direction relative to the heart.
Which vessels return blood?
topics.activity: Draw a heart with arrows showing blood going away through an artery and returning through a vein.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Electric current
topics.description: Electric current describes the rate at which electric charge flows through a conductor.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Identify electric current as the quantity measured in amperes.
evidence: Identifies the quantity measured in amperes.
misconceptions: Electric current is the same thing as the energy stored in a battery.
topics.question: What is measured in amperes in an electric circuit?
topics.answer: Electric current.
topics.explanation: Current measures how quickly electric charge passes a point in the circuit.
hints: Think about moving electric charge.
The rate of its flow is current.
topics.activity: Label the current in a diagram of a battery, switch and bulb; use only low-voltage classroom equipment.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Our Solar System
topics.description: The Solar System includes the Sun and objects that orbit it, including eight planets and many smaller bodies.
topics.locator: PDF p. 28, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Identify the Sun as the star around which Solar System planets orbit.
evidence: Identifies the Sun as the star around which planets in our Solar System orbit.
misconceptions: The Moon is the centre of the Solar System and the Sun orbits Earth.
topics.question: What star do the planets in our Solar System orbit?
topics.answer: The Sun.
topics.explanation: Gravity keeps planets in orbits around the Sun, the Solar System's star.
hints: Think of Earth's orbit.
Which star is at the centre of the Solar System?
topics.activity: Arrange labelled cards for the Sun and eight planets in order, noting that the model is not to scale.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Transverse and longitudinal waves
topics.description: In transverse waves oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel; in longitudinal waves they are parallel.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Classify a wave by comparing the directions of oscillation and travel.
evidence: Compares the direction of oscillation with the direction a wave travels.
misconceptions: All waves have particles vibrating in the same direction relative to travel.
topics.question: If a wave travels right while its particles oscillate up and down, is it transverse or longitudinal?
topics.answer: It is transverse.
topics.explanation: The oscillation is perpendicular to the direction in which the wave travels.
hints: Compare up-and-down motion with rightward travel.
Are the two directions perpendicular or parallel?
topics.activity: Draw a travelling wave arrow and separate arrows for transverse and longitudinal oscillations.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Complete combustion
topics.description: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon with sufficient oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water while transferring energy.
topics.locator: PDF p. 25, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Identify carbon dioxide and water as products of complete hydrocarbon combustion.
evidence: Identifies the products of complete hydrocarbon combustion.
misconceptions: Burning a hydrocarbon with enough oxygen makes only carbon and no water.
topics.question: What are the two main products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
topics.answer: Carbon dioxide and water.
topics.explanation: Hydrogen and carbon in the fuel react with oxygen; complete combustion transfers energy and forms these products.
hints: Consider the carbon and hydrogen in the fuel.
The products are carbon dioxide and water.
topics.activity: Write a word equation for complete combustion of methane using a supplied example; do not light a flame.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Decomposition and nutrient cycling
topics.description: Decomposers break down dead organisms and waste, returning materials that other organisms can use.
topics.locator: PDF p. 31, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain how decomposers return nutrients to the environment.
evidence: Explains a connection between decomposers and the availability of nutrients.
misconceptions: Materials in dead organisms disappear permanently from an ecosystem.
topics.question: How can decomposers help plants obtain nutrients?
topics.answer: They break down dead matter and waste, returning nutrients to the environment.
topics.explanation: The recycled materials can become available to plants and other organisms again.
hints: Think about what happens to dead leaves.
What is released as decomposers break them down?
topics.activity: Draw a cycle linking leaves, decomposers, soil nutrients and a growing plant.
materials: paper and pencil; add ordinary classroom materials as described

topics.name: Counting organisms in a habitat
topics.description: A tally records repeated observations and helps show how many organisms were seen in a selected area.
topics.locator: PDF p. 11, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Biological Science > Year 1 practices
objectives: Record and count observations of organisms using tally marks.
evidence: Turns repeated observations into a tally and checks the total.
misconceptions: A tally shows what is present in every habitat, including places that were not observed.
topics.question: A learner marks one tally for each of three birds seen in a garden. How many birds were recorded?
topics.answer: Three birds were recorded in that observation.
topics.explanation: Each mark represents one observation in the chosen place and time; the tally does not describe every habitat.
hints: Count the marks.
One mark stands for one bird.
topics.activity: From a safe distance, tally visible birds or plants in a small area for five minutes and describe where you observed.

topics.name: Comparing sound through materials
topics.description: A comparison of sound through different materials is more useful when the sound source and listening position stay similar.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Physical Science > Year 2 practices
objectives: Choose conditions to keep similar when comparing sound through different materials.
evidence: Suggests keeping the sound source and distance the same while comparing materials.
misconceptions: Changing the sound source and material together shows which material changed the sound.
topics.question: To compare sound through two barriers, what should stay the same as each barrier is changed?
topics.answer: Use the same sound source and keep its position and the listening position similar.
topics.explanation: Keeping other conditions similar makes the comparison of the materials easier to interpret.
hints: Change just the barrier.
What else could make the sound seem louder?
topics.activity: At a comfortable volume, listen to the same quiet sound through a sheet of card and a folded cloth, keeping positions similar.

topics.name: Measuring stretch
topics.description: Measuring an object's length before and after stretching can show how much its size changed.
topics.locator: PDF p. 9, Phase 1 (Years 0–3) > Physical Science > Year 3 practices
objectives: Calculate a change in length from measurements before and after stretching.
evidence: Subtracts an initial length from a stretched length using the same units.
misconceptions: A stretched object has changed by its entire final length.
topics.question: A soft elastic strip is 5 cm long before stretching and 8 cm long afterwards. How much did its length increase?
topics.answer: Its length increased by 3 cm.
topics.explanation: The increase is the stretched length minus the starting length: 8 − 5 = 3 cm.
hints: Compare the two lengths.
Subtract 5 from 8.
topics.activity: Measure a soft elastic strip before and after a gentle stretch; keep it away from faces and record both lengths.

topics.name: Checking temperature measurements
topics.description: Repeated temperature readings and careful instrument use help reveal disagreement or measurement error.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 4 practices
objectives: Suggest a repeat measurement and method check when temperature readings disagree.
evidence: Suggests rechecking readings and comparing the method when two temperatures differ.
misconceptions: A single reading must be correct even when another careful measurement differs.
topics.question: Two learners read the same water sample as 20°C and 24°C. What should they do next?
topics.answer: Measure again, check how each thermometer was read and compare the results.
topics.explanation: A repeat and a check of the instruments and reading method can reveal whether a reading was mistaken or conditions changed.
hints: Do the readings agree?
Repeat them and look for a difference in method.
topics.activity: Use two classroom thermometers to measure the same room-temperature water and compare readings after they settle.

topics.name: Controlling variables
topics.description: When comparing insulation, keep the containers, starting water temperature and time the same while changing the wrapping.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 5 practices
objectives: Identify a condition to control when comparing insulation materials.
evidence: Identifies one variable that must be controlled during a comparison.
misconceptions: A fair comparison can change the container, starting temperature and insulation all at once.
topics.question: Two wrapped cups are compared for insulation. Name one condition to keep the same.
topics.answer: Keep the starting water temperature the same, or keep the cups or time interval the same.
topics.explanation: Controlling other conditions makes it easier to attribute a difference in cooling to the wrapping.
hints: Only the wrapping should change.
Consider the cups, starting temperature or elapsed time.
topics.activity: Wrap identical cups with two materials, add the same amount of lukewarm water and compare temperatures after the same interval with adult supervision.

topics.name: Recording variation in leaf size
topics.description: A sample of leaf measurements can show variation within a plant species without assuming every individual is identical.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 6 practices
objectives: Describe the observed range of leaf lengths in a small sample.
evidence: Uses a measurement table to describe the range in a small sample.
misconceptions: Every leaf of the same species must have exactly the same length.
topics.question: A sample of leaves is 4 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm long. What range of lengths was observed?
topics.answer: The observed lengths range from 4 cm to 7 cm.
topics.explanation: The sample shows variation; other leaves could have different lengths outside this small sample.
hints: Find the smallest and largest values.
The smallest is 4 cm and the largest is 7 cm.
topics.activity: Measure fallen leaves from one identified species, record their lengths and draw a simple frequency chart without damaging plants.
materials: fallen leaves from one identified species

topics.name: Conduction, convection, and radiation
topics.description: Thermal energy can transfer by conduction, convection or radiation; radiation can travel through empty space.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Physical Science > Year 7 knowledge
objectives: Identify radiation as the way energy travels from the Sun through space.
evidence: Identifies radiation as the way energy reaches Earth from the Sun through space.
misconceptions: Thermal energy always needs matter between the source and the object.
topics.question: How does thermal energy from the Sun reach Earth across space?
topics.answer: By radiation.
topics.explanation: Electromagnetic radiation can travel through a vacuum; conduction and convection require matter.
hints: Space between the Sun and Earth is mostly empty.
Which transfer method can travel through a vacuum?
topics.activity: Draw three everyday examples and label conduction, convection and radiation; never look directly at the Sun.

topics.name: Checking speed measurements
topics.description: Repeated timing trials help reveal inconsistent results and improve confidence in a speed investigation.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Physical Science > Year 7 practices
objectives: Explain why repeated timings and method checks help assess inconsistent speed measurements.
evidence: Suggests repeating a trial and checking timing methods when results differ.
misconceptions: The fastest single timing is automatically the most reliable result.
topics.question: A toy car takes 4 seconds in one trial and 8 seconds in another over the same distance. What should you do before drawing a conclusion?
topics.answer: Repeat the measurement and check whether the car and timing method were consistent.
topics.explanation: Different readings may reflect changes in release, distance or reaction time; extra trials help identify the pattern.
hints: The two results are quite different.
Check the method and try more than once.
topics.activity: Roll a toy car along the same marked distance three times and record each time and how it was released.

topics.name: Separating inks by chromatography
topics.description: Paper chromatography separates some dissolved dyes as water carries them along paper at different rates.
topics.locator: PDF p. 19, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Physical Science > Year 8 practices
objectives: Use separated coloured spots as evidence that an ink may contain multiple dyes.
evidence: Uses the positions of separated coloured spots as evidence that an ink contained more than one dye.
misconceptions: Every colour of ink is necessarily made from a single dye.
topics.question: A water-based ink separates into a blue spot and a yellow spot on paper. What does that suggest?
topics.answer: The ink contained at least two dyes that separated.
topics.explanation: Dyes can move different distances because they interact differently with the paper and water.
hints: Count the separated colours.
More than one spot suggests more than one component.
topics.activity: Put a water-based marker dot on a paper strip above a shallow water line and watch water rise; keep the ink dot above the water at the start.

topics.name: Human Reproduction
topics.description: In human sexual reproduction, fertilisation joins an egg and sperm to form a zygote, which can develop into an embryo.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Biological Science > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Identify the egg and sperm as the reproductive cells that join at fertilisation.
evidence: Names the cells that join at fertilisation and the resulting zygote.
misconceptions: Fertilisation occurs when two body cells of any type join.
topics.question: Which two reproductive cells join during human fertilisation?
topics.answer: An egg cell and a sperm cell.
topics.explanation: Their genetic material combines in a single cell called a zygote, which can begin development.
hints: These are specialised reproductive cells.
One is an egg cell and the other is a sperm cell.
topics.activity: Label a simple diagram showing egg, sperm, zygote and embryo; no personal information is needed.

topics.name: Menstruation and the uterus
topics.description: In a menstrual cycle, the lining of the uterus can build up and later be shed as menstrual bleeding.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Biological Science > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Identify the uterus as the organ whose lining is shed during menstruation.
evidence: Identifies the uterus as the organ whose lining is shed during menstruation.
misconceptions: Menstrual bleeding is caused by the bladder shedding its lining.
topics.question: Which organ sheds its lining during menstruation?
topics.answer: The uterus.
topics.explanation: Menstrual bleeding includes tissue and blood from the uterine lining; the bladder is a different organ.
hints: Think about the organ involved in pregnancy.
It is the uterus.
topics.activity: On a teacher-provided anatomical diagram, label the uterus and indicate its lining; do not ask classmates about their bodies.

topics.name: Sampling an ecosystem with quadrats
topics.description: A quadrat marks a consistent area in which organisms or environmental features can be recorded and compared.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Biological Science > Year 8 practices
objectives: Explain why equal-sized sampling areas make habitat counts more comparable.
evidence: Explains why equal sampling areas make a comparison more meaningful.
misconceptions: Counts from sampling areas of different sizes can always be compared directly.
topics.question: Why use the same-sized quadrat in two different parts of a habitat?
topics.answer: The same-sized area makes counts more comparable.
topics.explanation: An unequal area could change the count even if the density of organisms stayed the same.
hints: Think about the area being sampled.
A larger area may contain more organisms simply because it is larger.
topics.activity: Use a string square to count a visible plant in several safe, accessible patches; avoid trampling plants or disturbing animals.

topics.name: Neutral atoms and electric charge
topics.description: A neutral atom has equal numbers of positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Use proton and electron counts to determine whether an atom is neutral.
evidence: Uses proton and electron counts to identify a neutral atom.
misconceptions: An atom with more protons than electrons has no net charge.
topics.question: An atom has six protons and six electrons. What is its net electric charge?
topics.answer: Its net charge is zero.
topics.explanation: The six positive proton charges and six negative electron charges balance.
hints: Compare the numbers of positive and negative charges.
Equal opposite charges cancel.
topics.activity: Draw a simple model of an atom with six protons and six electrons and label their charges.

topics.name: Conductors and insulators
topics.description: Conductors permit electric charge to move more readily than insulators; metals are usually good conductors.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Compare a metal conductor with an insulating plastic coating.
evidence: Classifies a common metal as a conductor and plastic as an insulator.
misconceptions: All solid materials conduct electricity equally well.
topics.question: Which is usually the better electrical conductor: copper wire or its plastic coating?
topics.answer: The copper wire.
topics.explanation: Copper allows charge to move readily, whereas the plastic coating restricts its movement.
hints: Consider which material is used inside the wire.
The metal is the conductor.
topics.activity: Sort pictures of copper wire, plastic coating and other common materials into predicted conductors and insulators; do not use mains electricity.

topics.name: Static electricity and sparks
topics.description: Electric charge can accumulate on an object's surface and exert forces on other objects.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Identify static charge as a possible cause of attraction after rubbing.
evidence: Recognises a build-up of charge as one possible cause of attraction after rubbing.
misconceptions: Only magnets can exert a force without touching.
topics.question: After a plastic comb is rubbed, it attracts small pieces of paper. What kind of charge build-up can cause this?
topics.answer: Static electric charge on the comb.
topics.explanation: Charge can accumulate on the comb and exert a force on nearby paper without direct contact.
hints: The comb is electrically charged.
The charge is static because it has built up on the surface.
topics.activity: Rub a clean plastic comb on a dry cloth, hold it near tiny paper pieces and record what happens.

topics.name: Voltage and current
topics.description: Voltage is the electric potential difference between two points; current is the rate of flow of electric charge.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish voltage measured in volts from current measured in amperes.
evidence: Distinguishes voltage measured in volts from current measured in amperes.
misconceptions: Volts and amperes measure the same quantity.
topics.question: Which quantity is measured in volts: electric potential difference or current?
topics.answer: Electric potential difference, also called voltage.
topics.explanation: Voltage describes a difference in electric potential; current measures charge flow and is measured in amperes.
hints: One unit is volts and the other is amperes.
Voltage is measured in volts.
topics.activity: Label volts and amperes on a diagram of a low-voltage battery circuit and match each unit to its quantity.

topics.name: Resistance and current
topics.description: Electrical resistance limits the movement of charge through a component; at the same voltage greater resistance reduces current.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Predict current when resistance changes while voltage remains constant.
evidence: Predicts a smaller current when resistance increases and voltage is held constant.
misconceptions: Adding resistance always makes more current flow through an unchanged-voltage circuit.
topics.question: If voltage stays the same and resistance increases, what happens to current?
topics.answer: The current decreases.
topics.explanation: A greater resistance opposes the flow of charge more strongly when the voltage is unchanged.
hints: Keep voltage fixed in the comparison.
Greater resistance makes charge flow less readily.
topics.activity: Use a supplied table of simulated circuit values to compare currents at the same voltage and different resistances.

topics.name: Electric fields
topics.description: An electric field is a region around a charged object where another charge experiences an electric force.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Explain how an electric field allows a charged object to exert a force at a distance.
evidence: Explains that a charged object can affect another charge without touching it.
misconceptions: Electric forces can act only when two objects touch.
topics.question: Why can one charged object exert a force on another charged object without touching it?
topics.answer: The second charge is in the electric field around the first.
topics.explanation: An electric field describes the region in which a charge can experience an electric force.
hints: Think about the space around a charged object.
What describes the electric force in that region?
topics.activity: Draw two charged objects and arrows to represent a possible attractive or repulsive force; label the diagram as a model.

topics.name: Ionic bonding
topics.description: An ionic bond is the attraction between positively and negatively charged ions after electrons are transferred.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain how attraction between oppositely charged ions holds an ionic compound together.
evidence: Explains that opposite ionic charges attract in an ionic compound.
misconceptions: An ionic bond forms because neutral atoms share all their electrons equally.
topics.question: What attracts sodium ions and chloride ions together in sodium chloride?
topics.answer: Opposite electric charges attract the positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions.
topics.explanation: Electron transfer produces ions with opposite charges, and their electrostatic attraction holds the ionic structure together.
hints: Consider the charges on the two ions.
One is positive and the other is negative.
topics.activity: Draw positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions alternating in a simple two-dimensional model; label it as a model.

topics.name: Covalent bonding
topics.description: A covalent bond involves atoms sharing electrons, commonly between non-metal atoms.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Identify shared electrons in a covalent bond.
evidence: Distinguishes shared electrons in a covalent bond from transferred electrons in ionic bonding.
misconceptions: All chemical bonds form by transferring electrons from a metal to a non-metal.
topics.question: What do atoms share when they form a covalent bond?
topics.answer: They share electrons.
topics.explanation: Shared electrons form the bond between atoms in a covalent molecule.
hints: The electrons are held in common by the atoms.
They are shared rather than transferred completely.
topics.activity: Draw two hydrogen atoms sharing a pair of electrons in an H₂ molecule using a simple dot model.

topics.name: Reading chemical formulas
topics.description: A chemical formula uses element symbols and subscripts to show the kinds and numbers of atoms in a molecule.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Count each kind of atom in a simple molecular formula.
evidence: Counts each kind of atom in a familiar molecular formula.
misconceptions: The subscript in a chemical formula counts every atom in the molecule.
topics.question: How many hydrogen atoms and oxygen atoms are in one H₂O molecule?
topics.answer: Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
topics.explanation: The subscript 2 applies to H; an O with no subscript represents one oxygen atom.
hints: Read the number immediately after each element symbol.
No subscript means one atom.
topics.activity: Draw and label models of H₂O and CO₂, counting atoms of each element.

topics.name: Balancing chemical equations
topics.description: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom in the reactants and the products.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 practices
objectives: Count atoms on both sides of an equation to check conservation of an element.
evidence: Checks conservation of atoms on both sides of a simple equation.
misconceptions: Balancing an equation requires changing the chemical formula of a substance.
topics.question: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many oxygen atoms are on each side?
topics.answer: There are two oxygen atoms on each side.
topics.explanation: One O₂ molecule has two oxygen atoms and two H₂O molecules contain one oxygen atom each.
hints: Count oxygen atoms on the left, then the right.
The coefficient 2 applies to each atom in H₂O.
topics.activity: Use counters in two colours to model the atoms on each side of 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O; do not perform the reaction.

topics.name: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
topics.description: Electromagnetic radiation includes radio waves, visible light and other types; it can travel through a vacuum.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Recognise radio waves and visible light as parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
evidence: Recognises visible light as one part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
misconceptions: Only visible light belongs to the electromagnetic spectrum.
topics.question: Are radio waves and visible light both types of electromagnetic radiation?
topics.answer: Yes, both are electromagnetic waves.
topics.explanation: They occupy different parts of a spectrum ordered by wavelength and frequency, and both can travel through a vacuum.
hints: Visible light is only one part of the spectrum.
Radio waves are another part.
topics.activity: Arrange cards for radio, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays in spectrum order using a reference diagram.

topics.name: Seeds and spores
topics.description: Many flowering plants reproduce using seeds, while ferns reproduce using spores.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 4 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish fern spores from the seeds produced by flowering plants.
evidence: Distinguishes a fern spore from a flowering plant seed in an example.
misconceptions: Every plant reproduces by making seeds.
topics.question: What does a fern produce for reproduction: spores or seeds?
topics.answer: Ferns produce spores.
topics.explanation: Ferns and flowering plants use different reproductive structures; flowering plants form seeds.
hints: Ferns are one of the plant groups that does not produce seeds.
Ferns produce spores.
topics.activity: Use teacher-provided pictures of a fern and a flowering plant to compare their reproductive structures; do not collect unknown fungi.

topics.name: Digestion begins in the mouth
topics.description: Teeth break food into smaller pieces and saliva begins chemical digestion in the mouth.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 5 knowledge
objectives: Describe the roles of teeth and saliva at the start of digestion.
evidence: Names a mechanical and a chemical contribution to digestion in the mouth.
misconceptions: Food only begins to change after it reaches the stomach.
topics.question: What two changes begin digestion in the mouth?
topics.answer: Teeth break food into smaller pieces and saliva begins chemical digestion.
topics.explanation: Breaking food mechanically and starting chemical digestion help prepare it for later digestion and absorption.
hints: Consider both teeth and saliva.
Teeth break pieces; saliva begins a chemical process.
topics.activity: Draw a labelled pathway from mouth to stomach and add one role for teeth and saliva; use no food in the activity.

topics.name: Capillaries and exchange
topics.description: Capillaries are very small blood vessels in tissues where materials can move between the blood and body cells.
topics.locator: PDF p. 17, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Identify capillaries as sites where substances move between blood and tissues.
evidence: Describes one role of capillaries in connecting blood with tissues.
misconceptions: Blood carries nutrients but cannot exchange substances with body cells.
topics.question: Where can substances move between blood and body cells in a tissue?
topics.answer: In tiny blood vessels called capillaries.
topics.explanation: Capillaries connect circulation with body tissues and allow substances to move between blood and cells.
hints: Think about the smallest blood vessels in tissues.
These vessels are capillaries.
topics.activity: Draw a heart, larger vessels and a capillary network next to a muscle, then use arrows to show nutrients reaching cells.

topics.name: Freshwater stores
topics.description: Most water on Earth is salty ocean water; freshwater is also stored in rivers, lakes, ice and underground.
topics.locator: PDF p. 15, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 6 knowledge
objectives: Name a freshwater store such as a lake, glacier or groundwater.
evidence: Names one freshwater store besides a river.
misconceptions: All of Earth's water is freshwater available to drink directly.
topics.question: Name one place where freshwater is stored besides a river.
topics.answer: Freshwater can be stored in a lake, glacier or underground.
topics.explanation: Freshwater occurs in several stores, and the form and accessibility of that water vary.
hints: Think about ice, lakes and water below the ground.
A lake or glacier is one example.
topics.activity: Sort fictional water-store cards into ocean water and freshwater stores, then identify one question about availability.

topics.name: Symbols in circuit diagrams
topics.description: Standard symbols can represent components in a circuit diagram so a reader can trace their connections.
topics.locator: PDF p. 14, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Physical Science > Year 6 practices
objectives: Explain how standard circuit symbols help readers identify components and trace connections.
evidence: Uses a key to distinguish a switch symbol from a lamp symbol in a provided diagram.
misconceptions: Every drawing of a circuit must show realistic pictures of the battery and bulb.
topics.question: Why use a key or standard symbols in a circuit diagram?
topics.answer: They let readers identify components and follow how they are connected.
topics.explanation: A shared set of symbols communicates the same component consistently without requiring a realistic picture.
hints: How can another reader recognise each component?
Standard symbols or a key identify the parts.
topics.activity: Using a supplied symbol key, draw a battery, switch and lamp in a closed loop; do not connect to mains electricity.

topics.name: Lunar eclipses and Moon phases
topics.description: A lunar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes into Earth's shadow; ordinary monthly phases result from the changing view of its sunlit half.
topics.locator: PDF p. 20, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Physical Science > Year 7 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish a lunar eclipse caused by Earth's shadow from an ordinary Moon phase.
evidence: Distinguishes Earth's shadow during a lunar eclipse from an ordinary Moon phase.
misconceptions: Every monthly Moon phase is caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.
topics.question: What makes a lunar eclipse different from an ordinary Moon phase?
topics.answer: During a lunar eclipse the Moon passes into Earth's shadow.
topics.explanation: Ordinary phases usually reflect the changing view of the sunlit half of the Moon as it orbits Earth.
hints: Where is Earth's shadow during an eclipse?
The Moon enters that shadow during a lunar eclipse.
topics.activity: Use a torch and two balls to compare an eclipse alignment with a normal phase model; never look directly at the Sun.

topics.name: Fungal spores and reproduction
topics.description: Many fungi reproduce by producing spores that can disperse and develop into new fungi under suitable conditions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 22, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Biological Science > Year 8 knowledge
objectives: Describe how a fungal spore can germinate and grow in suitable conditions.
evidence: Describes what fungal spores can do without treating them as plant seeds.
misconceptions: All spores are seeds made by flowering plants.
topics.question: What can a fungal spore do if it reaches suitable conditions?
topics.answer: It can germinate and grow into a new fungus.
topics.explanation: Fungi form spores as reproductive structures; a spore is not the same thing as a flowering plant seed.
hints: Think about how a new fungus may start.
A spore can germinate and grow.
topics.activity: Compare labelled diagrams of fungal spores and a flowering plant seed; do not collect or handle unknown fungi.

topics.name: Using fossils as evidence
topics.description: Fossils provide evidence about organisms that lived in the past and can be compared with living forms.
topics.locator: PDF p. 21, Phase 3 (Years 7–8) > Biological Science > Year 8 practices
objectives: Distinguish a visible fossil feature from inferences needing further evidence.
evidence: Draws a cautious inference from a fossil while recognising missing information.
misconceptions: A fossil can show every detail of an organism's behaviour and habitat.
topics.question: A fossil preserves a shell shape. What can that evidence directly tell a learner?
topics.answer: It can show the preserved shape of the shell.
topics.explanation: A shell can support further hypotheses, but a fossil alone may not reveal the organism's complete behaviour or environment.
hints: Separate what is visible from what is inferred.
The preserved shell shows its shape.
topics.activity: Compare two labelled fossil pictures and list one visible feature and one question that needs more evidence.

topics.name: Cells with and without nuclei
topics.description: Bacteria are prokaryotes whose genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus; typical plant and animal cells are eukaryotic and contain a nucleus.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Explain that bacterial DNA is present without being enclosed in a nucleus.
evidence: Distinguishes the location of genetic material in a bacterial cell from a eukaryotic cell.
misconceptions: Bacteria have no genetic material because they have no nucleus.
topics.question: Does a bacterial cell need a nucleus to contain genetic material?
topics.answer: No. Its genetic material is present but is not enclosed within a nucleus.
topics.explanation: Bacteria have DNA even though they are prokaryotes without a membrane-bound nucleus.
hints: Is having genetic material the same as having a nucleus?
Bacterial DNA is present without being enclosed in a nucleus.
topics.activity: Compare labelled diagrams of a bacterial cell and a plant cell, marking where genetic material is found.

topics.name: Infectious and non-infectious disease
topics.description: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread; non-infectious diseases are not caused by a transmissible pathogen.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Classify a disease caused by a transmissible virus as infectious.
evidence: Distinguishes the cause of an infectious illness from a non-infectious condition in a stated example.
misconceptions: Every illness can be passed from one person to another.
topics.question: Is a disease caused by a transmissible virus classified as infectious or non-infectious?
topics.answer: It is infectious.
topics.explanation: A virus is a pathogen, and an illness it causes can spread through relevant routes; many other conditions are non-infectious.
hints: Think about the cause named in the question.
A transmissible virus is a pathogen.
topics.activity: Sort fictional disease descriptions by whether a pathogen is identified; do not diagnose yourself or classmates.

topics.name: Immunity & Vaccines
topics.description: Vaccines can train the immune system to recognise a pathogen and build a protective response without requiring the target disease itself.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Explain how vaccination can prepare an immune response to a pathogen.
evidence: Explains immune memory in general terms without assuming complete protection for every person.
misconceptions: A vaccine has to cause the disease it is designed to protect against in order to work.
topics.question: How can a vaccine help the immune system respond to a pathogen later?
topics.answer: It helps the immune system recognise the pathogen and develop a protective response in advance.
topics.explanation: The immune system can develop specific immune memory; protection varies by vaccine and person and is not absolute.
hints: Think about preparing a response before later exposure.
The immune system can remember the target.
topics.activity: Draw a conceptual sequence linking vaccination, immune recognition and a later response; use no personal medical information.

topics.name: Comparing disease-prevention evidence
topics.description: Comparing infection rates across groups can be informative, but differences in exposure, age and study design also matter.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 9 practices
objectives: Compare fictional illness rates while recognising that counts alone do not establish causation.
evidence: Interprets a fictional comparison and identifies one reason it does not by itself prove causation.
misconceptions: One unadjusted comparison proves exactly why infection rates differ.
topics.question: In fictional groups of 100, five vaccinated people and 20 unvaccinated people became ill. What can be concluded from these counts alone?
topics.answer: The observed illness rate was lower in the vaccinated group in this example; the counts alone do not establish why.
topics.explanation: The groups may differ in exposure, age or other factors, so researchers use study design and further evidence to assess causes.
hints: First compare the observed counts.
Then ask whether the two groups may differ in other ways.
topics.activity: Calculate the two fictional percentages and list one additional piece of information needed for a fair comparison.

topics.name: Reading patterns in infection data
topics.description: A graph or table of cases over time can show changes in reported infections, but the data source and population matter.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 9 practices
objectives: Identify the highest reported count in a table without inferring its cause.
evidence: Identifies the day with the greatest stated count without inferring a cause.
misconceptions: A rise in reported cases automatically proves which intervention caused the change.
topics.question: A fictional table reports 2 cases on Monday, 5 on Tuesday and 3 on Wednesday. Which day has the highest reported count?
topics.answer: Tuesday, with 5 reported cases.
topics.explanation: Five is the largest of the three recorded counts; additional evidence is needed to explain the pattern.
hints: Compare the three numbers.
Which number is largest?
topics.activity: Plot the three fictional counts on a simple graph and write one question the graph cannot answer.

topics.name: Measuring current in a circuit
topics.description: An ammeter measures electric current through a component and is connected in series in the path being measured.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 practices
objectives: Identify where an ammeter is connected to measure current through a lamp.
evidence: Places an ammeter in series with a lamp in a low-voltage circuit diagram.
misconceptions: An ammeter must be placed across a battery without regard to its settings.
topics.question: Where should an ammeter be placed to measure current through a lamp in a simple circuit?
topics.answer: In series in the conducting path through the lamp.
topics.explanation: The current being measured flows through the ammeter and the lamp; real measurements require correctly rated equipment and supervision.
hints: The meter must be in the same path as the current through the lamp.
Place it in series with the lamp.
topics.activity: On a supplied low-voltage circuit diagram, place an ammeter symbol in series with the lamp; use paper only.

topics.name: Measuring voltage across a component
topics.description: A voltmeter measures potential difference between two points and is connected across the component of interest.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 practices
objectives: Identify where a voltmeter is connected to measure potential difference across a lamp.
evidence: Places a voltmeter across a lamp on a circuit diagram.
misconceptions: A voltmeter must replace the lamp in the only conducting path.
topics.question: Where is a voltmeter connected to measure the potential difference across a lamp?
topics.answer: Across the lamp, between its two terminals.
topics.explanation: Voltage is a difference between two points, so the meter compares the potentials at the component's ends.
hints: Which two points are being compared?
Connect the meter across the lamp.
topics.activity: Add a voltmeter symbol across a lamp in a supplied low-voltage circuit diagram; make no real electrical connections.

topics.name: Comparing current in a series circuit
topics.description: In a simple unbranched series circuit, current is the same through each component in steady operation.
topics.locator: PDF p. 26, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 practices
objectives: Predict current at two points in a steady unbranched series circuit.
evidence: Uses simulated readings to check whether a simple series path behaves consistently.
misconceptions: Current is used up by the first bulb, so less charge reaches the next component.
topics.question: In a steady unbranched series circuit, a simulated ammeter reads 0.2 A before the lamp. What should an ideal meter read after the lamp?
topics.answer: It should also read 0.2 A.
topics.explanation: Charge flows through one continuous path; the lamp transfers energy but does not use up electric charge.
hints: How many current paths are there?
In one unbranched path, the same current passes each point.
topics.activity: Use a supplied simulated circuit to compare current readings at two points and record what a mismatch might prompt you to check.

topics.name: Genes and protein production
topics.description: Many genes contain instructions used to make proteins; a gene's activity affects whether its protein is produced.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain how an active gene can provide instructions for making a protein.
evidence: Explains one relationship between a gene and the protein made from its instructions.
misconceptions: Genes determine traits without cells making or using any proteins.
topics.question: What can happen when a gene containing instructions for a protein is active?
topics.answer: The cell can use its instructions to make that protein.
topics.explanation: Proteins perform many cellular roles and contribute to characteristics; not every gene is active in every cell at every time.
hints: What do the instructions in many genes help the cell make?
They can guide the production of a protein.
topics.activity: Draw a simple model linking a gene's instructions, protein production and one stated cellular function.

topics.name: Proteins in cells
topics.description: Proteins perform a range of functions, including building structures, transporting substances and speeding up reactions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Give an example of a protein's structural, transport or chemical function.
evidence: Gives an example of a protein function without assuming all proteins do the same job.
misconceptions: Every protein has exactly the same function in the body.
topics.question: What is one role a protein can have in a cell or organism?
topics.answer: A protein can help build a structure, transport a substance or speed up a reaction.
topics.explanation: Different proteins have different shapes and functions; enzymes are one group of proteins that speed up reactions.
hints: Think about structure, transport or chemical reactions.
Some proteins act as enzymes.
topics.activity: Sort fictional protein role cards into structure, transport and reaction categories, allowing discussion of different examples.

topics.name: Phenotype and environment
topics.description: An organism's observable characteristics reflect interactions between its genetic information and environmental conditions.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 10 knowledge
objectives: Explain how genetic information and environmental conditions can influence an observed trait.
evidence: Explains how both genetic information and environment can influence an observed trait.
misconceptions: An observable trait must always be determined by genes alone.
topics.question: Why might two plants with similar inherited traits grow to different heights?
topics.answer: Differences in environmental conditions such as available water or light can influence growth.
topics.explanation: Observable characteristics can reflect inherited information together with conditions experienced during development.
hints: Compare both inheritance and growing conditions.
Water or light can affect growth.
topics.activity: Use two fictional plant profiles with similar inheritance but different growing conditions and suggest what additional measurements would help.

topics.name: Discrete and continuous trait data
topics.description: Some traits are recorded in distinct categories while others can vary across a range of numerical values.
topics.locator: PDF p. 29, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 10 practices
objectives: Distinguish a continuous measurement such as leaf length from a discrete category.
evidence: Classifies a stated measurement as continuous and a stated category as discrete.
misconceptions: Every observable trait must be recorded as one of a few fixed categories.
topics.question: Is leaf length measured in millimetres normally treated as continuous or discrete data?
topics.answer: It is treated as continuous data.
topics.explanation: Lengths can vary across a range, even though a measuring instrument records them to a chosen precision.
hints: Can length vary between whole-number measurements?
Length varies along a range.
topics.activity: Sort fictional plant traits into categories and measurements, then plot supplied leaf-length values without collecting personal information.

topics.name: Photosynthesis and respiration
topics.description: Photosynthesis uses light to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water; aerobic respiration releases usable energy from glucose with oxygen.
topics.locator: PDF p. 30, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Biological Science > Year 9 knowledge
objectives: Distinguish photosynthesis from aerobic respiration and recognise that plants carry out both.
evidence: Distinguishes the use of light in photosynthesis from the energy release of respiration.
misconceptions: Plants only photosynthesise and do not carry out cellular respiration.
topics.question: Do plants carry out cellular respiration as well as photosynthesis?
topics.answer: Yes. Plant cells respire as well as carrying out photosynthesis in light-absorbing tissues.
topics.explanation: Photosynthesis makes glucose; aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen to release energy needed for life processes.
hints: Think about how plant cells obtain usable energy.
They also respire.
topics.activity: Draw two separate arrow diagrams for photosynthesis and aerobic respiration, labelling inputs and outputs.

topics.name: Atomic mass number
topics.description: The mass number of an atom is the total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 atomic theory
objectives: Calculate mass number from the numbers of protons and neutrons.
evidence: Adds the proton and neutron counts without including electrons.
misconceptions: Mass number is the number of protons alone.
topics.question: An atom has 6 protons and 7 neutrons in its nucleus. What is its mass number?
topics.answer: Its mass number is 13.
topics.explanation: The mass number is the total of protons and neutrons: 6 + 7 = 13. The atomic number is 6 because it counts only protons.
hints: Which two particles in the nucleus contribute to mass number?
Add the 6 protons and 7 neutrons.
topics.activity: Draw a nucleus containing 6 protons and 7 neutrons. Label both the atomic number and mass number, and explain how they differ.

topics.name: Electron shells in the introductory atomic model
topics.description: In the introductory ground-state model for elements in the first three periods, electrons are placed in successive shells following the 2, 8, 8 pattern.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 atomic theory
objectives: Represent the ground-state electron arrangement of a neutral atom from the first three periods using the introductory shell model.
evidence: Places 11 electrons in a 2, 8, 1 arrangement and identifies the model as simplified.
misconceptions: All electrons in a neutral atom must be placed in a single shell.
topics.question: Using the introductory ground-state shell model, how are the 11 electrons of a neutral sodium atom arranged across its first three shells?
topics.answer: They are arranged 2, 8, 1.
topics.explanation: The first shell holds 2 electrons and the second holds 8 in this model, leaving 1 of sodium’s 11 electrons in the third shell. This is the ground-state arrangement in the introductory model for the first three periods.
hints: Place 2 electrons in the first shell and up to 8 in the second.
How many of the 11 electrons remain after placing 10?
topics.activity: Draw a simplified ground-state shell model for a neutral sodium atom, count the electrons in each shell and note that the diagram is a model.

topics.name: Valence electrons and bonding
topics.description: The valence shell is the outermost electron shell of an atom; its electrons take part in chemical bonding.
topics.locator: PDF p. 24, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 9 atomic theory
objectives: Identify valence electrons in an introductory shell diagram.
evidence: Identifies the outer shell and counts its electrons in a stated arrangement.
misconceptions: Valence electrons are always the electrons closest to the nucleus.
topics.question: An atom has electrons arranged 2, 8, 7 in three shells. How many valence electrons does it have?
topics.answer: It has 7 valence electrons.
topics.explanation: The outermost, or valence, shell is the third shell in this arrangement, and it contains 7 electrons.
hints: Find the outermost shell in the 2, 8, 7 arrangement.
The number in the last shell is 7.
topics.activity: Draw a simplified 2, 8, 7 shell diagram, circle the valence shell and explain which electrons can participate in bonding.

topics.name: Newton's First & Second Laws
topics.description: When the net force is zero, an object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity. For a nonzero net force, force, mass and acceleration are related by F = ma.
topics.locator: PDF pp. 26–27, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science; Year 10 forces and acceleration, building on the Year 9 net-force model
objectives: Use Newton’s First Law to describe motion under zero net force and apply F = ma to an unbalanced force.
evidence: Calculates acceleration using net force and mass, including the direction of the net force.
misconceptions: A moving object must always have a nonzero net force to keep moving at constant velocity.
The force in F = ma can be one force while ignoring other forces on the same object.
topics.question: A 2 kg trolley experiences a net force of 6 N to the right. What is its acceleration?
topics.answer: Its acceleration is 3 m/s² to the right.
topics.explanation: Newton’s Second Law gives a = F/m = 6 N ÷ 2 kg = 3 m/s², in the direction of the net force. When net force is zero, velocity remains constant.
hints: Use the net force rather than one individual force.
Divide 6 N by 2 kg and use the force direction.
topics.activity: On paper, show an 8 N force right and a 2 N force left on a 2 kg trolley. Find the net force and acceleration, then compare with zero net force.

topics.name: Newton's Third Law
topics.description: When two objects interact, each exerts a force of equal size and opposite direction on the other; the two forces act on different objects.
topics.locator: PDF p. 27, Phase 4 (Years 9–10) > Physical Science > Year 10 action–reaction force pairs
objectives: Identify both objects and the equal, opposite forces in a Newton’s Third Law pair.
evidence: Names the force on each object and explains that the pair acts on different objects.
misconceptions: An action–reaction pair consists of opposite forces that both act on the same object.
topics.question: A book pushes down on a table with a force of 4 N. What force does the table exert on the book?
topics.answer: The table pushes up on the book with a force of 4 N.
topics.explanation: The book’s downward contact force acts on the table, and the table’s equal upward contact force acts on the book. The forces are a pair because they act on different objects.
hints: The force from the table acts on the book.
Its size matches 4 N and its direction is opposite.
topics.activity: Draw the book and table separately. Add and label one arrow for the book’s force on the table and another for the table’s force on the book.

topics.name: Inherited traits in offspring
topics.description: A trait is a feature of an organism. Offspring can inherit characteristics from their parents, while individuals are not necessarily identical.
topics.locator: PDF p. 16, Phase 2 (Years 4–6) > Biological Science > Year 6 inheritance and variation
objectives: Recognise a trait described as passing from parents to offspring.
evidence: Identifies a stated parent-to-offspring trait as inherited without assuming offspring are identical.
misconceptions: Offspring must be exact copies of their parents.
topics.question: If a beak shape is passed from parent birds to their offspring, what kind of trait is it?
topics.answer: It is an inherited trait.
topics.explanation: An inherited trait is a characteristic passed from parents to offspring. The prompt states that this beak shape is passed on.
hints: Think about where the characteristic came from.
It was passed from the parents.
topics.activity: Draw a fictional parent bird and two offspring. Show the stated inherited beak shape, then add a note that offspring can also differ in other features.
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible drawing tool
